title: Your first three readable words
goal: Connect five vowel sounds to three words you can recognise.
scene: A blue sign, a house on a map, and an arrow pointing up.
notice: あ・い・う・え・お are the five vowel kana. あお has two sound beats: a-o. Let each vowel stay steady.

questions.prompt: Which word labels the blue colour?
why: いえ means house. Look for a-o.
うえ means above. Look for a-o.

questions.prompt: Which word has the sounds i-e?
why: うえ is u-e. Start with い for i-e.
あお is a-o. Start with い for i-e.

use: A friend points to a blue notebook. Type あお or a-o, or say it aloud and note the two sounds.
checks: I connected the word to blue.
I kept a and o as two beats.

title: Hear a house, hear an arrow
goal: Tell i-e and u-e apart by listening.
scene: A map has a house symbol and an upward arrow.
notice: Both words end in え. The first vowel changes the meaning: いえ is house; うえ is above.

questions.prompt: Listen: which meaning fits?
why: うえ means above; this model begins with i.
あお means blue; this model ends with e.

questions.prompt: Listen: which meaning fits this time?
why: House is いえ; hear the first u here.
Blue is あお; this model is u-e.

use: You hear u-e beside an arrow. Say or type the word, then name what helped you hear it.
checks: I identified above rather than house.
I noticed the first vowel changed.

title: Read a tiny map
goal: Read いえ and うえ without needing kanji.
scene: The house icon has the label いえ. An arrow above it has the label うえ.
notice: You can read these labels with vowel kana alone. Kanji are not required for this task.

questions.prompt: The label いえ belongs beside which symbol?
why: The upward label is うえ.

questions.prompt: Which kana starts the label meaning above?

use: Make a two-label mini map: house / above. Use kana, romaji, or describe your aloud reading.
checks: I matched both labels to their meaning.
I checked the first vowel in each word.

title: Make your first word card
goal: Write one meaningful two-kana word and check it.
scene: Create a little card for a blue object or a house.
notice: Choose one word. Try writing or typing before comparing. If you have no Japanese keyboard, romaji is welcome; handwriting can happen on paper.

questions.prompt: You want a card saying house. Which model fits?
Which order spells blue?
why: The model is a-o, not o-a.
あ then お spells あお.
Blue ends in お, not え.

use: Write one small word card on paper or type it here. State which meaning you chose and one thing you checked.
model: あお — blue / いえ — house
checks: I tried writing before comparing.
I checked the kana order against the model.

title: Say something you can point to
goal: Say a two-beat word with a meaning in mind.
scene: Point to a house picture or imagine something blue.
notice: Start with a word you want to say. Two beats is the aim here; a timer or readable transcript cannot check pronunciation.

questions.prompt: Which reading belongs to あお?
How many sound beats are in いえ?

use: Say あお or いえ while pointing to its meaning. Write a short note about which sounds you tried.
checks: I made an aloud attempt.
I kept the two vowels distinct when comparing with the model.

title: One extra beat changes the word
goal: Notice the held vowel in おばあさん.
scene: Two family labels look similar, but one has an extra あ.
notice: おばさん has four mora beats: お・ば・さ・ん. おばあさん has five: お・ば・あ・さ・ん. The extra あ is part of the word.

questions.prompt: Which word means grandmother?
why: おばさん means aunt. Check for the extra あ.
The extra あ makes おばあさん: grandmother.

questions.prompt: Which has five mora beats?
why: お・ば・あ・さ・ん: five.
お・ば・さ・ん has four.

use: Label a fictional family photo grandmother. Type kana or romaji, or say the five beats and describe your check.
checks: I chose grandmother rather than aunt.
I kept the extra あ beat.

title: Hear the extra vowel
goal: Listen for the difference between aunt and grandmother.
scene: You hear a family member mentioned in an audio label.
notice: Listen to the whole word. Replay the models to compare the shorter and longer vowel.

questions.prompt: Listen to this label. Who is named?
why: Aunt is the shorter おばさん.

questions.prompt: Listen to the second label. Who is named?
why: This is the family word おばさん.
Grandmother would include another あ beat.

use: Listen again to the two family labels, then say or write the shorter one from memory.
checks: I selected the shorter family label.
I compared it with the longer model after trying.

title: Spot the small っ
goal: Notice where a short consonant hold belongs in a word.
scene: A post-office label says きって: postage stamp.
notice: The small っ occupies a mora beat. In きって it marks a hold before t; it is not a separately spoken tsu. Large つ and small っ are different.

questions.prompt: Which word has a small っ?
why: きて has no small っ.
きって has small っ before て.

questions.prompt: How should the small っ work in きって?
why: A full tsu would be the large つ.
Hold the consonant for a beat before releasing te.
The hold is part of the word.

use: Make a stamp label and mark its beats: ki / hold / te. Kana or a beat description is fine.
checks: I distinguished small っ from large つ.
I placed the hold before て.

title: Write the difference you can hear
goal: Write or copy two forms carefully and explain one difference.
scene: A small sound difference deserves a visible place on your word card.
notice: Trying once and checking a specific detail is more useful here than filling a page with rushed copies.

questions.prompt: Which spelling means grandmother?
why: Keep the extra あ and final ん.

questions.prompt: Which character needs to be small in きって?
why: っ is the small hold marker.

use: Write おばさん / おばあさん or きって on paper or here. Explain the one detail you corrected.
model: おばさん / おばあさん / きって
checks: I made a first attempt before comparing.
I checked vowel length or small っ specifically.

title: Give the hold its own beat
goal: Say きって with a consonant hold rather than a full tsu.
scene: Imagine asking a post-office worker about a stamp; practise the item name first.
notice: Clap three mora beats: ki / hold / te. The middle beat prepares the t; avoid adding a full tsu vowel.

questions.prompt: Which beat plan fits きって?
why: That adds a full tsu vowel.
The hold gets its own mora beat.

questions.prompt: Which name has the held a vowel?
why: おばあさん contains the extra あ.
おばさん has the shorter vowel.
きって practises a consonant hold.

use: Say きって once, compare with the audio, and try it again. Note whether you held before t or added a vowel.
checks: I tried the word aloud before comparison.
I noticed the consonant hold rather than just checking the spelling.

title: A menu word you already know
goal: Read すし by connecting kana to a familiar food.
scene: You spot a short food label at a restaurant.
notice: か starts ka; さ starts sa. Two familiar words make the rows useful: かお is face and すし is sushi.

questions.prompt: Which label means sushi?
Which kana starts かお?
why: こ is ko; かお starts ka.
さ is sa; かお starts ka.

use: Imagine a menu label for sushi. Read or write it, then name the two sounds.
checks: I connected the label to sushi.
I read su-shi in the right order.

title: Hear su-shi and ka-o
goal: Match a short spoken word to its meaning.
scene: A friend points to a food picture, then a face picture.
notice: し is commonly romanised shi in learner materials. Listen for the vowel and consonant together.

questions.prompt: Listen. Which picture fits?
Listen again. Which picture now?

use: Say or type the word you heard for face. Compare only after your attempt.
checks: I matched ka-o to face.
I tried recall before replaying.

title: Read a word in three beats
goal: Decode せかい from a sequence of familiar kana.
scene: A poster has the word せかい: world.
notice: せ・か・い has three mora beats. Read one kana at a time, then connect the sounds into the word.

questions.prompt: What is the reading of せかい?
why: The first kana is せ, se.
Follow せ, then か, then い.

questions.prompt: Which word means face?

use: Add world to a tiny personal word list. Write its kana or romaji and its meaning.
checks: I read all three kana in order.
I connected the sound to world.

title: Write two useful labels
goal: Choose food or face and make a clear kana label.
scene: You are making two picture cards you can recognise tomorrow.
notice: Try one label, compare, then make a small correction. This is writing practice; typing can help recall but does not assess handwriting.

questions.prompt: Which order writes sushi?
why: す then し writes sushi.
The second sound should be し.

questions.prompt: Which spelling labels a face?
why: The second vowel should be お.
The first kana should be か.

use: Write すし and かお on paper or here. Explain one detail you checked against the models.
checks: I tried writing both words.
I checked the order and a character shape or sound.

title: Say a word you would choose
goal: Say すし or せかい with its meaning in mind.
scene: Choose the food you recognise or the word for the world you want to explore.
notice: You do not need a full sentence to practise a useful word. Say it, compare with the model, and name one next step.

questions.prompt: Which sounds make すし?
why: That reading belongs to せかい.

questions.prompt: How many mora beats does せかい have?
why: Each of these three kana has one beat.

use: Choose sushi or world. Say it aloud, then write the word or a brief note about your attempt.
checks: I spoke before comparing.
I checked the sound sequence rather than aiming for speed.

title: Read a cat and an octopus
goal: Use the first kana to distinguish two words ending in こ.
scene: A cat photo and an octopus menu picture both have short labels.
notice: ねこ and たこ both end in こ. Look closely at the first kana: ね is ne; た is ta.

questions.prompt: Which label belongs to the cat?
Which label belongs to the octopus?

use: Label a cat photo in a pretend message. Type kana, use romaji, or say the label and note its sounds.
checks: I chose cat rather than octopus.
I checked the first kana.

title: Hear ne-ko and ta-ko
goal: Hear which word is named when the ending stays the same.
scene: You listen to two picture labels with your screen partly covered.
notice: Listen for ne versus ta. The shared ko ending is not enough to identify the word.

questions.prompt: Listen: which picture is named?
Which picture is named now?

use: Listen once more, then say the word for octopus from memory and note the first sound.
checks: I identified ta rather than ne.
I tried the word before replaying.

title: Find summer on a word card
goal: Read なつ and distinguish つ from ち.
scene: A seasonal card shows a sun and the label なつ.
notice: なつ is na-tsu. The kana つ is tsu; ち is chi. This task introduces the sound contrast, without requiring a whole unfamiliar sentence.

questions.prompt: Which word says summer?
Which kana has the reading tsu?

use: Make a summer word card: kana or romaji plus meaning. Compare つ with ち before finishing.
checks: I connected なつ to summer.
I distinguished つ from ち.

title: Write labels you can tell apart
goal: Write ねこ and たこ and check the first character.
scene: Make two picture labels that will still make sense when mixed up.
notice: Choose one character detail to inspect. A correct typed answer shows recall, not verified pen strokes.

questions.prompt: Which word starts with ね?
Which word should go under an octopus picture?

use: Write both labels from memory, compare with the models, and describe one check or revision.
checks: I made two writing attempts.
I checked which first kana matched each picture.

title: A tiny picture tour in your own voice
goal: Name two pictures aloud and notice what you can recall.
scene: Show a friend a cat, something blue, or a sushi picture. Choose two labels.
notice: You have met several meaningful words. Choose two that you want to keep; pause and recall before listening again.

questions.prompt: Which reading labels a cat?
Which word would label a blue colour?

use: Name any two pictures aloud, then write the words or explain which sounds you checked.
model: ねこ / あお / すし / たこ
checks: I named two chosen pictures aloud.
I compared one specific sound with a model after trying.
